> 「如来得阿耨多罗三藐三菩提耶？如来有所说法耶？」……「无有定法名阿耨多罗三藐三菩提，亦无有定法如来可说。何以故？如来所说法，皆不可取、不可说，非法、非非法。」

The seventh section asks whether the Buddha got anything and whether he said anything. Both answers are no.

This is the point where a reader who has followed along begins to suspect the sutra of dismantling its own basis. If there is no dharma to attain and no dharma to teach, what have we been reading for six sections?

The section is not nihilistic. It is precise about which thing is being denied.

## 无有定法 denies the formula, not the criterion

定法 is a fixed thing: a settled standard, a rule that applies identically in all cases, an answer you can carry in your pocket. The mind wants exactly this — one method, guaranteed, transferable.

What is denied is that such a fixed dharma exists, *including* a fixed dharma called enlightenment. What is not denied: the way causes and conditions work, the possibility of seeing clearly, the difference between a mind that is free and one that is not.

The distinction is the difference between "there is no right answer" (which the text does not say) and "there is no answer that stays right regardless of the situation" (which it does).

## 不可说 is a statement about capacity, not a prohibition

The Buddha then talks for twenty-five more sections. So 不可说 cannot mean "say nothing".

The book's gloss: reality cannot be exhaustively framed by language. A finger pointing at the moon is not the moon, but the finger is not useless — it is simply not the destination.

The error the section targets is the identification of words with the thing: reading the menu and believing you have eaten.

## 非法、非非法 leaves both ends

非法: it is not a real, graspable dharma. 非非法: it is also not the case that there is no dharma at all, and anything goes.

Two denials in a row, and the second one is the one people skip. The first denial produces the mature-sounding conclusion that everything is empty and nothing can be said. The second denial forbids that conclusion: the absence of a fixed dharma is not the absence of the dharma.

This is 中道 in its technical sense — not compromise, not "both sides have a point", but leaving two extremes with precision. Compromise averages positions. This refuses both.

## 一切贤圣，皆以无为法而有差别

The section's last line is easily read as an afterthought. It is the answer to an obvious objection: if there is no fixed dharma, why do the sages differ? Why do the stages of the path exist?

无为法 — the unconditioned — is one. The differences among the sages are differences in the clarity of the one who perceives it, not in what is perceived.

The book's image: one moon, several viewers, some with cloud in the eye. The moon has not divided itself into grades. The seeing has.

Which also explains why the sutra can spend the next sections on the four fruits without contradicting itself here: the fruit is a description of how much cloud has cleared, not a rank conferred.

## The test

Take the method you trust most — a practice, a framework, a way of working that has served you.

Ask: is it a 定法, or is it a 方便? Do you apply it because the situation calls for it, or because it is yours?

If you feel a small resistance at that question, that resistance is the fixed dharma. The method is probably fine.
